 Rohan Naahar is a News Writer for Collider. From Francois Ozon to David Fincher, he'll watch anything once.
 He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. He also writes obsessively about the box office, charting the many hits and misses that are released weekly, and how their commercial performance shapes public perception. In his time at Collider, he has also helped drive diversity by writing stories about the multiple Indian film industries, with a goal of introducing audiences to a whole new world of cinema.

 After a solid month-long run in theaters, one of the most divisive movies of 2026 is heading home. Interestingly, the film is headlined by the star of another highly controversial film, also distributed by the same company earlier this year. The first film emerged as a runaway hit, grossing $135 million worldwide against a reported $28 million budget, buoyed by positive reviews and a provocative central conceit. Starring Robert Pattinson and Zendaya , the movie in question is The Drama . Pattinson's latest film has essentially matched The Drama 's box-office performance domestically, and has yet to be released in most overseas markets. It will, however, become available to rent and purchase on PVOD platforms this week.

 The film was released theatrically in September, and has so far grossed more than $46 million at the domestic box office against a reported budget of under $15 million. The chances of it touching the $50 million mark seem slim, given that it's playing in only around 175 theaters nationwide. The Drama ended its domestic box-office run with $48 million, and is now sitting at a "Certified Fresh" 76% score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes. Pattinson and Zendaya were also a part of Christopher Nolan 's record-breaking epic The Odyssey , and will soon be seen in Denis Villeneuve 's hotly anticipated sci-fi threequel Dune: Part Three .

 Which idea grabs you most in a film?

 How do you like your story told?

 What do you want from a film's ending?

 How do you feel about a film that takes its time? 
 Pace is a choice. Some films sprint. Others let tension accumulate slowly, deliberately. 
 A I love a slow build when the payoff is going to be seismic. Patience for a devastating reveal.

 C Epic runtime does not scare me. If the material demands three hours, give me three hours.

 ★ Best Picture, 2020 
 Parasite 
 Bong Joon-ho, 2019 
 A film that hides its true intentions until the moment it is ready to reveal them. 
 You are drawn to films that operate on several levels at once, that begin in one genre and quietly, brilliantly migrate into another. Bong Joon-ho's Parasite is a film about class, desire and the architecture of inequality that manages to be darkly funny, deeply suspenseful and genuinely shocking across a single extraordinary running time. Your instinct is for cinema that rewards close attention and punishes assumptions, right up to its devastating final image.

 The first film not in the English language to win Best Picture, in the Academy's
 92-year history to that point.
 It took four Oscars in one night: Picture, Director, Original Screenplay and International
 Feature.
 It won the Palme d'Or at Cannes in 2019 by a unanimous jury vote, the first Korean film
 to do so.
 The Park family's modernist house was not a location. It was built from scratch on an
 outdoor lot.
 Reads between the lines 
 Loves a reveal 
 Attention to detail 
 ★ Best Picture, 2023 
 Everything Everywhere All at Once 
 Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert, 2022 
 A film that refuses to choose between being entertaining and being meaningful. 
 You want it all, and this one gives you all of it. The Daniels' Everything Everywhere All at Once is among the most maximalist films ever made: action comedy, multiverse science fiction, family drama, existential crisis, and an emotional core that sneaks up on you in the middle of the chaos. You respond to ambition. Being overwhelmed is the design, not the side effect, because the feeling of being crushed by infinite possibility is exactly what the film is about.

 Seven Oscars, including three acting wins for Michelle Yeoh, Ke Huy Quan and Jamie Lee
 Curtis.
 Michelle Yeoh became the first Asian woman to win Best Actress.
 The visual effects were handled by a team of fewer than ten people, most of them
 self-taught.
 Ke Huy Quan had all but left acting for two decades before this role brought him back.
 Wants everything 
 Big swings 
 Soft center 
 ★ Best Picture, 2024 
 Oppenheimer 
 Christopher Nolan, 2023 
 A film about the gap between what we can do and what we should do. 
 You are drawn to cinema on a grand scale, films that treat history not as a backdrop but as a force, then place their characters inside that force and watch what happens. Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer sits inside one of the most consequential moments in human history and refuses to look away from it. You want your films to feel important without being self-important, earning their ambition through craft and the gravity of the subject. This one is enormous, complicated, and offers no easy comfort. 
 From the Collider file 
 Seven Oscars, including Nolan's first wins for directing and for Best Picture.
 Cillian Murphy and Robert Downey Jr. both took their first Academy Awards for it.
 Kodak engineered a black-and-white 65mm stock that did not previously exist so Nolan could
 shoot those sequences on IMAX.
 A three-hour, R-rated drama about theoretical physics that passed 950 million dollars
 worldwide.
 Thinks in decades 
 Scale and weight 
 No easy comfort 
 ★ Best Picture, 2015 
 Birdman 
 Alejandro G. Iñárritu, 2014 
 A film doing something that probably should not be possible. 
 You are drawn to films that foreground their own construction, where the how of the filmmaking becomes part of the what it is about. Alejandro G. Iñárritu's Birdman, stitched to appear as one continuous take, is cinema examining itself through the cracked mirror of a fading actor's ego. You respond to formal daring. Michael Keaton's performance and Emmanuel Lubezki's restless camera make something unlike anything else: a film about creativity, relevance, self-destruction and never quite knowing whether your work means anything at all. 
 From the Collider file 
 Four Oscars, among them Best Picture and Best Director for Iñárritu.
 Emmanuel Lubezki's win here was the middle of three consecutive cinematography Oscars,
 after Gravity and before The Revenant.
 Antonio Sánchez's improvised drum score was ruled ineligible for the score category,
 which caused a minor uproar.
 The long-take illusion was built from a handful of extended shots joined by hidden cuts.
 Formally daring 
 Camera as character 
 Ego and art 
 ★ Best Picture, 2008 
 No Country for Old Men 
 Joel and Ethan Coen, 2007 
 A film that treats dread as a form of meaning. 
 You are drawn to cinema that trusts silence, refuses to explain itself, and lets unease do the talking. The Coen Brothers' No Country for Old Men is about the arrival of a new kind of evil: implacable, arbitrary, and indifferent to the moral frameworks we use to make sense of things. It is one of the most tightly controlled films ever made, and that control is the source of the terror. You want your films to haunt you rather than comfort you, and you have no interest in a resolution that would be a lie.

 Four Oscars: Picture, Director, Adapted Screenplay, and Supporting Actor for Javier Bardem.
 Adapted from Cormac McCarthy's 2005 novel, with much of his dialogue carried over
 intact.
 Carter Burwell's score runs about sixteen minutes and is nearly inaudible by design.
 Roger Deakins was nominated twice that year, for this and The Assassination of Jesse James,
 and won for neither.
 Trusts silence 
 Dread over answers

 But we're talking about Primetime , the controversial thriller based on the television series To Catch a Predator 's short-lived run in the mid-2000s. Directed by Lance Oppenheim , who also co-directed the recent word-of-mouth sensation You Can See Everything , the movie holds a "Certified Fresh" 86% score on Rotten Tomatoes. The aggregator website's consensus reads, "Turning the camera's scrutinizing eye back onto To Catch a Predator 's journalistic legacy, Primetime interrogates the slippery boundary between justice and lurid spectacle with crackling style and an outstanding Robert Pattinson." Also featuring Merritt Wever , Skyler Gisondo , and Phoebe Bridgers , Primetime will debut on the PVOD market on November 3. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.
